subject: {{first_name}}
note: Reframed from offshore-staffing positioning to outcome-led offers. Not deployed to PlusVibe.

variations.name: Admin overhead reduction
variations.angle: Cut back-office labor spend 50-70% without dropping coverage
paragraphs: {{first_name}},
most healthcare ops leaders we talk to say back-office labor is one of the hardest costs to keep flat as volume grows.
A few teams in your space have been replacing onshore admin headcount with dedicated remote FTEs at roughly 50-70% lower all-in cost — same hours, same systems, direct management.
Not sure if that's on your radar. Open to a short call to hear how you're handling admin overhead at {{company_name}}?

variations.name: Margin protection
variations.angle: Fix the cost side when reimbursement pressure hits
paragraphs: {{first_name}},
when reimbursement or payer rates move against you, most teams can't fix revenue overnight — but they can fix labor on the back office.
We've seen healthcare operators keep the same patient-facing coverage while cutting regional admin spend by half or more with dedicated remote teams.
Worth a quick conversation to see if that model fits {{company_name}}?

variations.name: RCM / denials capacity
variations.angle: Clear AR backlog without another US hire
paragraphs: {{first_name}},
curious how {{company_name}} is handling revenue-cycle volume right now — denials, follow-ups, payer intake, that kind of work.
A lot of groups we speak with are adding capacity there without another $55-65k regional hire by using dedicated remote staff who already know US healthcare workflows.
Open to a brief chat?

variations.name: Cost math
paragraphs: {{first_name}},
quick one — back-office roles that run $55-70k all-in regionally often land around $1,600/month as a dedicated full-time remote hire (salary, loads, equipment included).
That's usually a 50-70% swing on the same function: scheduling, AR follow-up, payer intake, admin support.
Not sure if you're actively looking at that. Happy to walk through the math for {{company_name}} if useful.

variations.name: Onshore burnout relief
variations.angle: Move repetitive admin off your US team's plate
paragraphs: {{first_name}},
a pattern we keep hearing from healthcare operators: onshore staff are stuck doing repetitive admin — calls, scheduling, documentation — and patient-facing work suffers.
Some teams pull that work onto dedicated remote FTEs so the US side stays focused on higher-value work.
Is that something {{company_name}} is running into, or mostly handled already?

variations.name: Low-risk pilot
variations.angle: Start with 5-10 people, no deposit, first month no-cost exit
paragraphs: {{first_name}},
for teams nervous about changing how they staff the back office, the lowest-friction path we've seen is a 5-10 person pilot on one workflow — AR, scheduling, payer intake, whatever hurts most.
No recruiting fees upfront, month-end invoicing only, and if the first month doesn't work you can walk away without paying.
Open to a short call to see if a pilot like that would even make sense for {{company_name}}?

variations.name: Competitive pressure
variations.angle: Peers already scaling back office remotely
paragraphs: {{first_name}},
more DME, RCM, and provider groups are keeping regional headcount lean and pushing repeatable back-office work to dedicated remote teams.
Main driver is usually margin — same coverage, materially lower labor line.
Curious whether {{company_name}} is exploring that or planning to keep everything onshore.

variations.name: Hiring difficulty
variations.angle: Skip the local talent gap for process-driven roles
paragraphs: {{first_name}},
when local hiring for back-office roles keeps stalling, some healthcare teams stop waiting on the regional market.
They build dedicated remote FTEs for process-heavy work — AR, scheduling, intake — at a fraction of a US hire, with HIPAA-trained staff.
How's local hiring been for those roles at {{company_name}}?
